papers.title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
papers.abstract: Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair, in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org.

papers.title: Adversarial Problems and the Limits of Uniform Resolution
papers.abstract: A general method of resolution can take part in forming problems once their language represents the method itself. A fixed formation rule gives each sound resolver a presentation it cannot answer. Admitting the diagnosis yields a sound successor with an instance of its own. For standard arithmetical theories $\mathrm{T}$, the instance is $\mathsf{HA}$-provably equivalent to $\mathrm{Con}(\mathrm{T})$. A theory that decides its own instance asserts a false sentence. The $m$-th iterated independence question is equivalent to the instance $m$ stages later. No effective admission policy with consistent union closes the regress. A noncomputable answer function resolves all program indices, while a false assertion of resolution supplies no warrant. At feasible scale, bounded self-consistency is cheap. A clocked G\"odel sentence gives an unconditional gap relative to its short binary description, but no superpolynomial lower bound in the window size. The arithmetic identity motivates studying bounded consistency of the successor theory, as in a conjecture of Pudl\'ak. We state its finitely axiomatized case and prove that it implies $\mathcal{NP}\ne\mathrm{co}\mathcal{NP}$. The conjecture motivates a feasible analogue, but does not establish all clauses of the unbounded barrier.

papers.title: Non-Expansive Fuzzy Modal Logic Has Uniform Interpolation
papers.abstract: Fuzzy logics with truth values in the unit interval vary in their choice of propositional connectives and their semantics, ranging from just minimum and maximum as in Zadeh logics to truncated addition and subtraction as in {\L}ukasiewicz logics or their extensions with truth constants, known as Pavelka logics. In the more specific world of fuzzy modal logics, non-expansive fuzzy modal logic has recently been proposed as a sweet spot between {\L}ukasiewicz (more precisely, Pavelka) and Zadeh fuzzy modal logic; it restricts {\L}ukasiewicz propositional connectives to have one argument constant, equivalently extends the Zadeh propositional base with constant shift operators. It retains reasonable expressiveness both in practical terms and abstractly; in particular, it characterizes the standard notion of behavioural distance on fuzzy Kripke frames. At the same time, it allows for satisfiability checking in the same complexity as for its two-valued correspondent (the modal logic K, or the description logic ALC), in contrast to the notorious computational hardness of {\L}ukasiewicz modal logic. In the present work, we show that non-expansive fuzzy modal logic admits uniform interpolation, a key property in modularization, information hiding, summarization, and other applications that fails for both {\L}ukasiewicz (or Pavelka) and Zadeh modal logic.

papers.title: Choosing What to Observe: Higher-Order Obstructions in Horn Abduction
papers.abstract: An explanation may exist in every complete context yet be impossible to select from the information observed. We study this distinction in finite propositional Horn abduction with integrity constraints. Observations are sufficient when each report admits one hypothesis set that is consistent and entails the manifestation in every compatible context. We characterize sufficiency by minimal context families with no common explanation. Their variable spans form a canonical hypergraph whose transversals are exactly the sufficient observation sets. The characterization recovers classical discernibility for unique explanations and supports composition across independent components. Minimal obstructions have unbounded cardinality even for acyclic rules, while rectangular explanation families admit a tight bound given by their largest choice domain. With circuit-defined contexts, sufficiency is $\Pi_3^P$-complete and selecting at most $k$ observable variables is $\Sigma_4^P$-complete, already for unrestricted contexts and acyclic rules. The selection reduction makes observation choices enforce globally fixed existential commitments. Explicit contexts reduce both tasks to NP-complete problems; tabulated explanation families make sufficiency polynomial. These results connect explanatory choice, information requirements, and representation cost.

papers.title: Guard Analysis and Safe Erasure Gradual Typing: a Type System for Elixir
papers.abstract: We formalize a new type system for Elixir, a dynamically typed functional programming language of growing popularity that runs on the Erlang virtual machine. Our system combines gradual typing with semantic subtyping to enable precise, sound, and practical static type analysis, without requiring any changes to Elixir's compilation pipeline or runtime. Type soundness is ensured by leveraging runtime checks -- both implicit, from the Erlang VM, and explicit, via developer-written guards. Central to our approach are two key innovations: the notion of "strong functions", which can be assigned precise types even when applied to inputs that may fall outside their intended domain; and a fine-grained analysis of guards that enables accurate type refinement for case expressions and guarded function definitions. While type information is erased before execution and not used by the compiler, our "safe erasure" gradual typing strategy maintains soundness and expressiveness without compromising compatibility or performance. This work lays the theoretical foundation for Elixir's new type system, outlines its integration into recent versions of the language, and demonstrates its effectiveness on large-scale industrial codebases.

papers.title: Expressivity Results for Structured Argumentation Frameworks with Uncertain Rules and Premises
papers.abstract: Modelling qualitative uncertainty in formal argumentation is essential both for practical applications and theoretical understanding. Yet, most existing work focuses on abstract models of argumentation under uncertainty. Following a recent trend in the literature, we tackle the open question of studying plausible instantiations of these abstract models. To do so, we root the uncertainty of arguments in their components in structured models: rules and premises. Our main conceptual contribution is to provide an intuitive notion of comparative expressivity suitable for both abstract and structured formalisms. Roughly, one formalism for arguing with qualitative uncertainty is at least as expressive as another if the former can generate the same set of abstract argumentation frameworks (completions) as the latter. On the technical side, we prove negative and positive results comparing the expressivity of abstract and structured models of argumentation with uncertainty. These results concern incomplete abstract argumentation frameworks and their extension with dependencies on the abstract side, and ASPIC$^+$, assumption-based argumentation (ABA) and deductive argumentation on the structured side.

papers.title: DeFAb: A Dataset for Grounded Scientific Discovery through Defeasible Abduction
papers.abstract: A theory can accommodate a counterexample by adding an exception. The harder problem is deciding how far the exception should extend and which predictions should survive. We present DeFAb, a dataset and symbolic verification framework built from curated biological knowledge in the Gene Ontology. Models fill gaps in a theory or propose exceptions to its rules. A verifier checks the consequences of each edit, allowing different solutions to receive credit. Simple symbolic repairs solve all 336 tasks in the released evaluation panel. This result exposes a limitation of the revision test. An exception tied to one entity can succeed without identifying a pattern that applies to other cases. We develop a contextual task that requires an exception to reach the relevant cases and preserve predictions elsewhere. Two planned studies compare training with verified and rejected examples, and revision with and without feedback about consequences. DeFAb makes the scope of a proposed explanation testable, providing a controlled step toward studying theory revision in scientific reasoning.

papers.title: Shapes from Examples: Foundations of Shape Learning in Recursive SHACL
papers.abstract: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, making automatic shape learning essential for knowledge graph applications. We investigate the well-known fitting approach to this task: given sets P and N of positive and negative example nodes from an input graph, compute a shape expression C, possibly using shape names defined in a recursive shape catalogue, that validates at every node in P and none in N. We focus on the case where C is written in a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the Description Logic ELI*. For the catalogue, we consider the well-founded, stable, and supported semantics. We address fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems, and obtain polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.

papers.title: A Decision Procedure for Probabilistic Kleene Algebra with Angelic Nondeterminism
papers.abstract: In Ong et al.~(2025), a new finite automaton model with probabilistic and nondeterministic transitions was introduced, along with a corresponding regular expression language. The key difference from previous approaches is that nondeterminism is formalized in terms of multisets instead of powersets. Automata and expressions are interpreted over the space of probability distributions over multisets of strings with finite multiplicities. The main result of that paper was a full Kleene theorem showing that the two formalisms are equally expressive. In this paper we give a decision procedure for the semantic equivalence of two automata or expressions. The algorithm is based on polyomial algebra and makes use of Gr\"obner basis techniques for ideal membership testing.

papers.title: Formal Foundations for Controlled Stochastic Activity Networks
papers.abstract: We introduce Controlled Stochastic Activity Networks (Controlled SANs), extending classical SANs with explicit control actions and policies for stochastic discrete-event and real-time systems. The framework combines nondeterminism, probabilistic branching, and stochastic timing through controlled automata, controlled probabilistic automata, and controlled stochastic automata. At the nondeterministic level, we distinguish structurally available controls from behaviorally admissible transitions and establish a constructive modeling-power result: every decidable, effectively finitely branching controlled automaton with finite activity and control sets and a finite nonempty initial-state set admits a computable, well-behaved controlled activity network realization whose reachable restriction is effectively isomorphic to the original. We define memoryless, finite-memory, stack-augmented, and tape-augmented policies, investigate their language-theoretic expressiveness, and develop behavioral equivalences including bisimulation and stochastic isomorphism. At the probabilistic level, contingent activity-indexed control assignments and an activity-generation law yield a discrete-time Markov decision process (DTMDP) representation; conversely, every conventional DTMDP admits a single-activity representation. Under Markovian assumptions, controlled stochastic automata admit continuous-time Markov decision process (CTMDP) projections, and conventional CTMDPs admit single-activity representations. Randomized-policy correspondences follow the adopted product-form convention. These results provide a semantic basis for verification, reward optimization, policy synthesis, and potential applications to reinforcement learning, safety-critical control, and agentic AI.

papers.title: Extracting total Amb programs from proofs
papers.abstract: We present a logical system CFP (Concurrent Fixed Point Logic) supporting the extraction of nondeterministic and concurrent programs that are provably total and correct. CFP is an intuitionistic first-order logic with inductive and coinductive definitions extended by two propositional operators: Restriction (binary), a strengthening of implication, and a unary operator for total concurrency. The source of the extraction is formal CFP proofs, the target is a lambda calculus with constructors and recursion extended by a constructor Amb (for McCarthy's amb) which is interpreted operationally as globally angelic choice and is used to implement nondeterminism and concurrency. The correctness of extracted programs is proven via an intermediate domain-theoretic denotational semantics. We demonstrate the usefulness of our system by extracting a nondeterministic program that translates infinite Gray code into the signed digit representation. A noteworthy feature of CFP is the fact that the proof rules for restriction and concurrency involve variants of the classical law of excluded middle that would not be interpretable computationally without Amb. This is a revised and extended version of the conference paper presented at ESOP 2022 with the same title that contains full proofs of all major results.
